The single-account evaluation order: implicit deny by default, explicit deny first, then SCP/RCP, resource-based, permissions boundary, session policy, identity-based. Quote the flow and the final-decision rules.
Does an explicit deny in any policy type override every allow? Which sentence says so?
Is the root user subject to IAM identity-based policies at all, and which policy types do limit it (SCP, RCP)?
In the same account, is an allow in a resource-based policy enough on its own (no identity-based allow needed), and does the reverse hold?
Cross-account: must both the caller's identity-based policy and the resource's resource-based policy allow the action? Who is the principal that the resource policy must name?
Permissions boundary: it sets the maximum and never grants; the effective permission is the intersection; does it limit what a resource-based policy grants to the same user or role session?
Which identities can carry a permissions boundary (users, roles) and which cannot (groups, service-linked roles)?
SCPs: they limit but never grant; they apply to every principal in member accounts including the root user; they do not affect the management account or service-linked roles.
RCPs: what they limit (resource-based policies of supported services), which services were supported at launch, and that they never grant access.

demand.question: Trust policy versus permissions policy: the trust policy is the role's resource-based policy naming who may assume it; the permissions policy says what the session may do. Quote both definitions.
Which two permissions are checked when a principal assumes a role (sts:AssumeRole in the identity policy and the trust policy), and when is the identity-policy allow implicit within the same account?
Temporary security credentials: they expire, are not stored with the identity, include a session token, and cannot be reused after expiry. Quote the 'why use them' list.
Comparison of the STS operations: who can call each (user, role, root), MFA support, session duration ranges, whether a policy is required (GetFederationToken) and whether they support role chaining.

Instance profile: a container for one role; an EC2 instance has at most one instance profile; the instance obtains rotated temporary credentials from the instance metadata; the application needs no keys.
iam:PassRole: a user must be allowed to pass a role to a service (EC2, Lambda); PassRole is not an API call; what else is needed (the role's trust policy naming the service).
Service-linked role: created and owned by the service, its trust policy is fixed, it cannot be deleted while in use, and no permissions boundary applies.
Service role versus service-linked role: who creates it, who may edit the permissions and trust policy.
The confused deputy problem: ExternalId in the trust policy for third-party cross-account access; aws:SourceArn and aws:SourceAccount for service principals.
Can you switch to a role that requires an ExternalId in the Management Console? Which paths do work (CLI, API)?
Which assume-role methods do not count as role chaining (AssumeRoleWithSAML, AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity, instance profile credentials) and so keep the longer duration?
Cross-account access with a role versus with a resource-based policy: with a role the caller gives up its own permissions; with a resource-based policy it keeps them. Quote the comparison.
Which services support resource-based policies (S3, SQS, SNS, Lambda, KMS, Secrets Manager, ECR, API Gateway, EFS, DynamoDB) and which common ones do not; where the table lives.
AWS managed, customer managed and inline policies: reuse, versioning, strict one-to-one relationship of inline policies, deletion with the identity; when AWS recommends each.
Groups: cannot be nested, are not principals (cannot appear in a Principal element), a user can belong to a limited number of groups, groups cannot own roles.
Root user: the tasks that require root credentials, the best practices (MFA, no access keys, do not use for daily work), and how to lock it down.
Centralized root access: delete root credentials of member accounts from the management account and run privileged tasks with short sessions (sts:AssumeRoot, its maximum duration).

Callvale decision: role on the instance (chosen) vs an IAM user with a key per workload vs only moving the key out of the code. Facts needed: instance-profile credentials are temporary and rotated automatically; access keys are long-term; AWS best practice says use roles for applications on EC2.

Callvale: IAM users with MFA in two groups until stage 3. Facts: groups hold policies for several users; a user can be in several groups; MFA can be enforced with a condition; Identity Center is the later replacement.
Callvale: lock the root user. Facts: enable MFA on root, delete root access keys, use root only for the listed privileged tasks, do not share the password.
